prompt: What does a denylist need to know in order to work?

choices.text: The valid format of each field
choices.why: That is what an allowlist knows. A denylist never describes the valid values.

choices.text: Every bad value, in advance
choices.why: Right, and nobody knows them all. The input was written by people who never read the list.

choices.text: Which user sent the request
choices.why: Who sent it is an access question, not a validation question.

choices.text: The database the value will be stored in
choices.why: The storage has nothing to do with what the list must predict.

prompt: The old booking form refuses <, >, ; and --. Which of these does it accept? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the date 2026-11-31
choices.why: No forbidden character in it, and November has 30 days.

choices.text: the clinic paulista
choices.why: Plain letters; and there is no clinic on Paulista.

choices.text: a booking with no phone at all
choices.why: A missing field becomes an empty string, which contains nothing forbidden.
This one contains --, so the denylist refuses it, for the wrong reason.

prompt: Why is `<` the wrong thing to look for when a phone number arrives?

choices.text: Phones never contain symbols
choices.why: Some people type +, spaces or hyphens. That is a format question, not a danger question.

choices.text: Python escapes angle brackets automatically in every string it handles
choices.why: Python does no such thing; templates escape, strings do not.

choices.text: Whether a character is dangerous depends on where the value goes next
choices.why: Right. At the input the useful question is whether this is a valid phone; the output handles its own context.

choices.text: Angle brackets are only dangerous in passwords
choices.why: They are harmless in passwords, which are hashed and never shown.

prompt: Where does a short denylist still earn its place?

choices.text: Over an open field, like a list of leaked passwords
choices.why: Right. It refuses known values inside a space that is otherwise open, which is the one job it does well.

choices.text: As the only check on a date field
choices.why: A date has a shape, and a parser checks it far better.

choices.text: Instead of escaping, on fields shown as HTML
choices.why: Escaping by context is the defence there; lesson 4 explains it.

choices.text: On the clinic field, listing every clinic that closed or never existed
choices.why: Four open clinics are easier to list than every name that is not one.

prompt: Put the five questions an allowlist asks of a field in the order the lesson gives.
items: is it one of the allowed values or formats?

prompt: Which call checks that a pattern describes the whole of a string?

choices.text: re.search
choices.why: search finds the pattern anywhere, so a valid phone followed by junk passes.

choices.text: re.match
choices.why: match anchors only the start; the end is free.

choices.text: re.fullmatch
choices.why: Right. The pattern must be all of the string.

choices.text: re.findall
choices.why: findall lists every occurrence; it says nothing about what surrounds them.

prompt: Why are the four clinics checked with `clinic in CLINICS` rather than with a regular expression?

choices.text: Regular expressions cannot match lower-case letters
choices.why: They match lower case perfectly well.

choices.text: A set is faster, and speed is the only thing that matters in a web form
choices.why: Speed is irrelevant at four values. The argument is correctness.

choices.text: When the valid values fit in a list, membership has no edge cases
choices.why: Right. True or false, and nothing to get wrong; a pattern is for values too many to list.

choices.text: Flask requires sets for form fields
choices.why: Flask has no opinion about how you validate.

prompt: `\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}` accepts `2026-11-31`. What catches it?

choices.text: A stricter regular expression with month lengths
choices.why: Possible in theory and unreadable in practice, and it still forgets leap years.

choices.text: Parsing it with date.fromisoformat
choices.why: Right. The parser knows how many days November has, and it raises ValueError.

choices.text: Escaping the hyphens
choices.why: The hyphens are not the problem; the day is.

choices.text: Nothing; the database refuses it later
choices.why: The booking list in this lesson refuses nothing, and a later refusal is a worse error message anyway.

prompt: In Python, the pattern ^[0-9]{11}$ accepts "11987654321\n", because $ also matches just before a final ___.
Which pattern refuses a phone written in full-width digits?

choices.why: \d matches any Unicode decimal digit, full-width included.
Right. The class names the ten ASCII digits and nothing else.
\w is wider still: letters and underscores too.
The dot matches any character at all.

prompt: digits.py prints `int(phone)` for the eleven full-width digits. What number does it print?
A function validates `value` and then stores `value.strip().lower()`. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing; tidying after the check is harmless
choices.why: The stored value is a different string, and nobody checked that one.

choices.text: lower() is slow on long strings
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: The stored value was never checked
choices.why: Right. Canonicalise first, check the canonical form, keep exactly what was checked.

choices.text: strip() removes the digits of a phone
choices.why: strip removes surrounding whitespace only.

prompt: Match each expression from digits.py to what it printed.
A name field should accept what people type on any keyboard. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Refuse anything outside ASCII letters
choices.why: That refuses João and Conceição, which is most of Vereda's patients.

choices.text: Normalise to NFKC first, then validate it
choices.why: Right. Decide the canonical form first, then check and keep exactly that.

choices.text: Validate the raw value, then normalise it before storing
choices.why: That stores a value nobody checked.

choices.text: Accept anything, because names have no format
choices.why: A name still has a length and a set of characters it should not contain, such as control characters.

prompt: An exam file name arrives as input. Which check holds?

choices.text: Refuse any name that contains ..
choices.why: A denylist again: it checks the text, not the file the name resolves to.

choices.text: Refuse names longer than 64 characters, or with more than one dot
choices.why: Length says nothing about which directory the path ends in.

choices.text: Accept it if it ends in .pdf
choices.why: The extension says nothing about where the file is.

choices.text: Resolve it, then confirm it is still inside exams/
choices.why: Right. The resolved path is the canonical form; lesson 14 does this with Path.resolve() and is_relative_to().

prompt: Against the old form, how many of the nine tests failed?
What does `@pytest.mark.parametrize` do in test_app.py?

choices.text: It runs one test per pair of values
choices.why: Right. One function, seven cases, seven lines in the report.

choices.text: It runs the tests in parallel to save time
choices.why: pytest runs them one after another here.

choices.text: It skips the test when a value is missing
choices.why: Nothing is skipped; every pair runs.

choices.text: It generates random values to try
choices.why: The values are the seven written in the list, every time.

prompt: Why does each refusal test also check `response.get_json() == {"error": f"invalid {field}"}`?

choices.text: To make sure the response is JSON and not HTML
choices.why: It does check that, as a side effect; the point is which field it names.

choices.text: It must name the field that was wrong
choices.why: Right. A status check alone passes a 400 about the wrong box, and sends the patient after the wrong mistake.

choices.text: pytest fails tests that do not read the body
choices.why: pytest has no such rule.

choices.text: To store the error message in the database
choices.why: Tests read the response; they store nothing.

prompt: Why did nobody using the old form notice that it checked nothing?

choices.text: The form showed a warning nobody read
choices.why: There was no warning to show.

choices.text: Patients always typed invalid data
choices.why: Most typed correct data, which is exactly why nobody noticed.

choices.text: A denylist never gets in the way of correct data
choices.why: Right. The good booking passes, so the form looks fine to everybody who uses it properly.

choices.text: The tests were never run
choices.why: There were no tests before this lesson; that is a different problem.

prompt: Where does the lesson put the validation, and how often does it run?

choices.text: In every function that uses a field, each time
choices.why: A scattered check is the one somebody forgets on the new route.

choices.text: At the boundary where data enters, once
choices.why: Right. Past the boundary the code receives a Booking and never asks again.

choices.text: In the database, through constraints
choices.why: Constraints are a useful second layer; the lesson validates at the route.

choices.text: In the browser, before the form is sent
choices.why: The browser is the client's; lesson 3 says why that cannot be the check.

prompt: Why does `validate` return a `Booking` instead of the dictionary it received?

choices.text: Dataclasses use less memory than dictionaries
choices.why: Memory is not the argument.

choices.text: Flask cannot serialise dictionaries
choices.why: jsonify serialises dictionaries all day long.

choices.text: The type says the fields were checked
choices.why: Right. Code that receives a Booking knows validation happened, and a raw dict stands out in review.

choices.text: Booking encrypts the phone number
choices.why: It stores the phone as text; nothing is encrypted.

prompt: Why does the fixed version not need a separate check for a missing phone?

choices.text: None fails like any wrong value
choices.why: Right. A missing field is None, and absent and wrong are refused by the same line.

choices.text: Flask refuses JSON bodies with missing keys
choices.why: Flask hands over whatever JSON arrived.

choices.text: The phone is optional in the fixed version
choices.why: It is required; the test for a missing phone passes.

choices.text: The dataclass fills it with an empty string
choices.why: validate raises before any Booking is built.

prompt: The error body says `invalid phone` and nothing else. Why not echo the value and the rule back?

choices.text: JSON cannot carry the original value
choices.why: It could; the choice is deliberate.

choices.text: Echoing it would make the response too large
choices.why: A phone number is a few bytes.

choices.text: The patient already knows the rule
choices.why: The form shows the rule; the response does not need to explain how to probe it.

choices.text: The field's name is enough for the form
choices.why: Right. The form highlights the box, and an echoed value is one more thing to escape; echoing input back into a response is how the next flaw starts.

prompt: `request.get_json(___=True)` returns None for a body that is not JSON, so validate refuses it like any other bad input.
A clinic name passed the allowlist. Can it now go straight into HTML, SQL or a shell command?

choices.text: Yes: validated data is safe everywhere
choices.why: Validation says the value means what it claims; it does not prepare it for each place.

choices.text: No: each of those places needs its own handling
choices.why: Right. Lessons 4 to 6 are about those places.

choices.text: Only into SQL, because the database checks types
choices.why: Types do not stop text from being read as SQL; lesson 5 explains.

choices.text: Only into HTML, because browsers ignore bad markup
choices.why: Browsers interpret markup eagerly; lesson 4 explains.

prompt: A new field arrives: the patient's CPF, eleven digits with a check digit at the end. Which validation fits the lesson best?

choices.text: Refuse it if it contains letters or symbols
choices.why: A denylist: it accepts eleven digits that are not a CPF.

choices.text: Accept any 11 characters, since the database stores text
choices.why: Length alone is one question of five.

choices.text: Decide the canonical form, fullmatch [0-9]{11}, then verify the check digits
choices.why: Right. Canonical form, format, and then the rule a parser would know, like a date's calendar.

choices.text: Use \d{11} with re.match
choices.why: Two mistakes: \d takes full-width digits and match leaves the end open.

prompt: A colleague adds a second route, `/bookings/<id>` with PUT, that copies the JSON into the stored booking. What should the review ask first?

choices.text: Does it go through validate, like the POST does?
choices.why: Right. A second route that skips the boundary undoes the whole lesson.

choices.text: Does it return 200 or 204?
choices.why: A detail of the protocol; the open door is the missing validation.

choices.text: Is PUT faster than POST?
choices.why: Not a meaningful difference, and not a security question.

choices.text: Does it log the request body?
choices.why: Logging is lesson 15's subject, and it may be the wrong thing to log.

prompt: Match each value to the allowlist question that refuses it first.

pairs.left: the phone sent as the number 11987654321
